cloze.text: On radiographs, the {{c1::external oblique ridge}} is a {{c2::radiopaque}} line on the external surface of the mandible, running {{c3::anterior from the ramus across the molars}}.
The {{c1::internal oblique ridge}} (also called the {{c2::mylohyoid}} ridge) is a radiopaque line on the internal surface of the mandible, running along the {{c3::premolar and molar apices}}.
On radiographs, the internal oblique ridge is usually positioned {{c1::below::above / below}} the external oblique ridge.
The {{c1::submandibular fossa}} is a {{c2::radiolucent}} band running inferior to the {{c3::mylohyoid line}} and the apices of the molars.
{{c1::Nutrient canals}} are vertical, thin radiolucent lines near the teeth that may be mistaken for {{c2::bone fractures}}.
The {{c1::mandibular canal}} is a radiolucent horizontal band outlined by a thin line of {{c2::cortical bone}}.
The mandibular canal carries the {{c1::inferior alveolar}} nerve and arteries.
The mandibular canal stretches from the {{c1::mandibular foramen}} to the {{c2::mental foramen}}.
Amalgam appears {{c1::completely radiopaque}} (solid white/bright) because {{c2::X-rays cannot penetrate metal}}.
Gold — whether a crown, inlay or onlay — appears {{c1::completely radiopaque}} (solid white) due to its {{c2::high density}}.
Composite typically appears {{c1::radiopaque}}, but its opacity varies significantly with its composition, e.g. the amount of {{c2::filler particles}}.
{{c1::Retention pins}} appear as thin, distinct radiopaque lines within a restoration; they {{c2::stabilize the restoration}}.
Base material appears {{c1::slightly radiopaque}} — fainter/more translucent white than metallic restorations; it is used to {{c2::protect the pulp}}.
Gutta-percha appears {{c1::slightly radiopaque}} — a distinct, slightly less dense white line within the root; it is used to {{c2::fill root canals}} during root canal therapy.
{{c1::Silver points}} are metallic points used to {{c2::obliterate canals}} during endodontic therapy; they appear radiopaque, as solid white thin lines within the root canal space.
Porcelain appears {{c1::slightly radiopaque}}: in a porcelain-fused-to-metal crown the metal core is a {{c2::solid radiopaque center}} and the porcelain a {{c3::slightly less radiopaque lining}}.
Orthodontic appliances (braces, bands, wires) appear {{c1::radiopaque}} — distinct white structures — due to their {{c2::metallic composition}}.
Dental implants appear radiopaque and typically resemble a {{c1::screw}} or cylinder, due to their metallic nature and {{c2::threaded design}}.
{{c1::Occlusal}} caries are harder to detect on radiographs because of the {{c2::superimposed structures}} of the tooth.
{{c1::Recurrent}} caries appear under restorations.
Caries visible on a radiograph are usually {{c1::more::more / less}} severe than they appear on the radiograph.
Interproximal caries, Incipient (Class I): {{c1::only in enamel, less than ½ way into enamel}}.
Interproximal caries, Moderate (Class II): {{c1::only in enamel, more than ½ way into enamel}}.
Interproximal caries, Advanced (Class III): {{c1::enamel + dentin, less than ½ way into dentin}}.
Interproximal caries, Severe (Class IV): {{c1::enamel + dentin, more than ½ way into dentin}}.
The radiographic pattern of periodontal bone loss is either {{c1::horizontal}} or {{c2::vertical}}.
In health, the alveolar crest should be {{c1::parallel}} with the CEJ.
Radiographs do not show bone loss in the {{c1::facial and lingual}} regions — only at the {{c2::interproximal alveolar crest}}.
Radiographic bone levels confirm that disease has occurred but do not show whether it is {{c1::active}}; to see changes, {{c2::compare past and present radiographs}}.
The {{c1::gingival level}} is not visible on a radiograph, but decreased bone level helps predict the {{c2::recession}} level.
Calculus is {{c1::not a disease}}, but it contributes to the disease process.
Widening of the PDL space can be caused by {{c1::periodontal diseases}} or {{c2::trauma}}.
{{c1::External resorption}}: root surface is lost with trauma such as {{c2::orthodontic therapy}}.
A root fracture appears as a {{c1::horizontal or vertical}} crack.

mcq.question: On a mandibular periapical radiograph, a thin vertical radiolucent line is seen in the bone near the teeth. The patient reports no trauma. This most likely represents:
mcq.explanation: Nutrient canals are thin vertical radiolucent lines near the teeth that may be mistaken for bone fractures. The mandibular canal is a HORIZONTAL radiolucent band; the internal oblique ridge is radiopaque.

mcq.question: A bitewing shows a solid white amalgam with a fainter, translucent white layer between the restoration and the pulp. This layer is most likely:
mcq.explanation: Base material protects the pulp and is slightly radiopaque — fainter than metallic restorations. Recurrent caries under a restoration would be radiolucent (dark), not white; gutta-percha is in the root canal.

mcq.question: An interproximal lesion extends through the enamel and less than halfway into the dentin. How is it classified radiographically?
mcq.explanation: Advanced (Class III) = enamel + dentin, less than ½ into dentin. Severe (Class IV) is more than ½ into dentin; Classes I–II are enamel only.

mcq.question: Which statement about radiographic assessment of periodontal disease is correct?
options: A. Radiographs show bone loss on the facial and lingual surfaces
B. One radiograph shows whether the disease is active
C. The gingival level is visible on the radiograph
D. Bone loss is seen only at the interproximal alveolar crest
mcq.answer: D. Bone loss is seen only at the interproximal alveolar crest
mcq.explanation: Radiographs show interproximal crest levels only, not facial/lingual bone. Bone levels confirm disease has occurred but not that it is active — that needs comparison of past and present radiographs. Gingiva is not visible.

mcq.question: Increasing the milliamperage (mA) will primarily affect which aspect of a dental radiograph?
mcq.explanation: Increasing mA increases the number of x-rays produced, resulting in a darker image due to increased density.

mcq.question: Which exposure factor has the greatest influence on radiographic contrast?
mcq.explanation: Higher kVp produces more penetrating x-rays, creating an image with low contrast (many shades of gray). Lower kVp gives high contrast (black/white image). (Book wording "source-to-film distance" and "a film with low contrast" changed to receptor/image — the exam no longer uses "film".)

mcq.question: Which radiographic error causes an image to appear too light?
options: A. Inadequate exposure time or mA
mcq.answer: A. Inadequate exposure time or mA
mcq.explanation: A radiograph that is too light is often due to too little exposure (low mA or too short an exposure time). (Book says "causes a film to appear too light" — reworded to "image"; the exam no longer uses "film".)

mcq.question: A radiograph shows elongation of the maxillary central incisors. This error was likely caused by:
mcq.explanation: Elongation results from too little vertical angulation — the beam is not directed steeply enough. (Option C was "Film reversal" in the book.)

mcq.question: Which anatomical landmark appears as a radiopaque "U"- or "J"-shaped structure superior to the maxillary molars?
options: B. Zygomatic process of the maxilla
mcq.answer: B. Zygomatic process of the maxilla
mcq.explanation: The zygomatic process of the maxilla appears as a U- or J-shaped radiopaque structure above the roots of the maxillary molars.

mcq.question: What is the effect of increasing kVp on the number and energy of x-rays produced?
mcq.explanation: Higher kVp increases both the penetrating ability and the quantity of x-rays produced.

mcq.question: Which structure appears as a radiolucent area between the maxillary central incisors and is a normal finding?
mcq.explanation: The incisive foramen appears as a normal round radiolucency between the central incisors. It's the exit point of the nasopalatine nerve.

mcq.question: Which landmark appears as a radiolucent curved structure in the posterior mandible?
mcq.explanation: The mandibular canal appears as a radiolucent band running below the molars, housing the inferior alveolar nerve.

mcq.question: A radiograph shows overlapping of proximal surfaces. What likely caused this error?
mcq.explanation: Incorrect horizontal angulation causes x-rays to miss the interproximal spaces, resulting in overlapping contact points. (Option D was "Reversed film" in the book.)

mcq.question: Which best describes stochastic effects of radiation exposure?
options: A. Effects that have a threshold dose before occurring
B. Effects that increase in severity with dose
C. Effects that occur by chance and increase in probability with dose
D. Immediate tissue damage following exposure
mcq.answer: C. Effects that occur by chance and increase in probability with dose
mcq.explanation: Stochastic effects, such as cancer or genetic mutations, have no threshold and the probability increases with dose, but severity does not.

mcq.question: What is the process by which x-rays remove electrons from atoms and may lead to tissue damage in the body?
mcq.explanation: Ionization occurs when x-rays eject electrons from atoms, producing charged particles (ions), which can cause biological damage.

mcq.question: What term describes the time period between radiation exposure and the appearance of a clinical effect?
mcq.explanation: The latent period is the time elapsed between radiation exposure and the first observable clinical sign or symptom of damage.

mcq.question: How does gutta-percha typically appear on a dental radiograph?
options: D. Completely radiolucent with a radiopaque outline
mcq.explanation: Gutta-percha, used to fill tooth canals in root canal therapy, typically appears slightly radiopaque on a radiograph — less dense than metallic restorations but clearly visible.

mcq.question: What is the Maximum Permissible Dose (MPD) for an occupationally exposed person per year?
mcq.explanation: For an occupational person, the Maximum Permissible Dose is 5 rem/year, which is equivalent to 50 mSv/year.

mcq.question: Which type of radiation effect has a probability of occurrence that increases with dose, but its severity is not dose-dependent?
mcq.explanation: Stochastic effects, such as cancer, are characterized by an increased probability of occurrence with a higher dose, but the severity of the effect (e.g., how severe the cancer is) does not depend on the dose.
